title: Sicilian Defence for Black
description: Meet 1.e4 with 1...c5. Learn why Black plays the Sicilian, the Open Sicilian main line, a short look at the Najdorf and the Dragon, what to expect after 2.c3 and 2.Nc3, and clear plans for Black.

moves.comment: The Sicilian Defence. The two sides now have different pawn plans, so the game is often sharp and decisive results are more common.

steps.intro: After 1.e4, Black answers with the c-pawn, not the e-pawn. The pawn on c5 keeps an eye on d4.

moves.comment: The Sicilian Defence.

hints: Use a pawn.
It is the pawn on c7. Push it two squares to c5.
steps.intro: White has played 1.e4. Black to move. Play the Sicilian: push the c-pawn two squares.
A black pawn on c5 attacks the squares b4 and d4. It stops White from simply putting a pawn on d4.

points: Against 1.e4 many players copy with 1...e5, which is solid and balanced
1...c5 makes the position unbalanced on purpose, so both sides play for a win
Lichess lists this as the Sicilian Defense
The pawn on c5 watches d4, so White cannot easily build a big center with d4
Say that sharp does not mean bad: Black must know the plans, not only the moves
mistakes: Thinking 1...c5 is a sleepy move
Copying White's moves instead of making a plan
Forgetting that the c-pawn guards the d4 square
questions: Which square does the pawn on c5 watch?
How is this different from 1...e5?
Why might a player want an unbalanced game?

lessons.title: The c-pawn for the d-pawn trade

moves.comment: Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn.
Now the c-file is half-open for Black: there is no black pawn on it. White still has the e4 pawn in the center.

steps.intro: Watch the pawns. White pushes d4. Black takes it with the c-pawn. White takes back with a knight. Now the c-pawn is gone, so Black has a half-open c-file for a rook.

moves.comment: Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn.

hints: Use a pawn.
Take the pawn on d4 with the pawn on c5.
steps.intro: White has pushed d4. Black to move. Capture the pawn on d4 with your c-pawn.
The black c-pawn was traded on d4. Black has no c-pawn, so a black rook on the c-file can look down the file as far as White's pawn on c2.

points: In the main line White gives up the d-pawn and Black gives up the c-pawn
White is left with a pawn on e4 in the center; Black has a pawn on d6 and a half-open c-file
Black keeps two center pawns (d6, e7) against White's one (e4).
Black's trade: White has more space, Black has a half-open file and good piece play
Use the board: count pawns on each side of the center
Keep it simple: this is why both sides have chances
mistakes: Saying the half-open file is only good for White
Forgetting that after cxd4 Black can still attack the knight with pieces
Thinking the trade of pawns makes the game equal and boring
questions: Which black pawn disappears from the board?
Which white pawn disappears?
On which file does Black now have a half-open file?

moves.comment: White develops and prepares d4.
The pawn guards e5 and opens the road for the bishop on c8.
Black takes the center pawn.
White recaptures with the knight.
The knight attacks the e4 pawn.
White defends e4 and develops. Now Black picks a setup.

steps.intro: This is a very popular road, often called the Open Sicilian. White plays Nf3 and d4. Black plays ...d6, takes on d4, then develops the knight to attack e4. White answers with Nc3.

moves.comment: The pawn guards e5 and opens a diagonal for the bishop on c8.

hints: Use a pawn.
It is the pawn in front of the bishop on c8. Push it one square to d6.
steps.intro: White has played 2.Nf3. Black to move. Guard the e5 square with a pawn: push the d-pawn one square.

moves.comment: Develops a piece and attacks the e4 pawn.

hints: Use a knight.
Move the knight on g8 to f6. It will attack the pawn on e4.
steps.intro: White has put a knight on d4. Black to move. Develop the knight from g8 to a square where it attacks e4.

hints: Answer 1.e4 with a pawn move on the c-file.
Then play d6, take on d4, and put the g8 knight on f6.
steps.intro: Play the Open Sicilian main line as Black.

points: Players call lines with 2.Nf3 and 3.d4 the Open Sicilian; Lichess names the position after 4...Nf6 Sicilian Defense: Modern Variations, Main Line (B54)
White opens the center with d4 and the d-pawn is traded
The order matters: ...d6 first guards e5 and keeps the c8 bishop free, then ...cxd4, then ...Nf6 hits e4
5.Nc3 defends e4, so Black does not win a pawn
After 5.Nc3 Black chooses a setup: Najdorf with ...a6, Dragon with ...g6, and others
Lichess groups the move order with d6 under Modern Variations of the Sicilian
mistakes: Playing ...cxd4 before ...d6 is not wrong, but can allow other ideas for White
Forgetting that ...Nf6 attacks the e4 pawn so White must react
Moving the c8 bishop too early with ...Bg4 (in the Open Sicilian) or ...Bd7 and wasting time
Starting an attack before castling
questions: Which black pawn move guards e5?
Which black piece attacks the pawn on e4 after ...Nf6?
How does White defend the e4 pawn?

moves.comment: The Najdorf Variation. Black keeps the options ...e5 and ...b5 for later.

steps.intro: In the Najdorf Black plays the quiet-looking 5...a6. The pawn takes away the b5 square from White's knight and bishop.

moves.comment: The Najdorf Variation. The pawn controls b5.

hints: Use a pawn.
It is the pawn on the a-file. Push it one square to a6.
steps.intro: White has played 5.Nc3. Black to move. Play the Najdorf move: push the a-pawn one square.
The pawn on a6 attacks b5, so White cannot easily put a knight or a bishop there. It also prepares later pawn pushes.

points: This is only a first look: the Najdorf is one of the most heavily studied lines, so do not try to teach it all
Lichess calls it the Najdorf Variation
The idea of 5...a6: the pawn controls b5, so White's knight or bishop cannot go there safely
The pawn also prepares ...b5 and ...e5 later
Tell students that strong players spend years on this line, and that is fine
mistakes: Playing ...a6 without knowing why
Thinking a rook-pawn move is always a waste of time
Memorizing long lines before learning the plans
questions: Which square does the pawn on a6 control?
Which white pieces want to use b5?
Which two pawn pushes does ...a6 prepare?

moves.comment: The Dragon Variation.
White develops the bishop.
The dragon bishop arrives.
This pawn guards e4 and keeps Black's knight out of g4, so the bishop on e3 is safe.
Black castles first.
Black attacks the knight on d4.

steps.intro: In the Dragon Black plays 5...g6 and puts the bishop on g7. From g7 it looks along a long diagonal. White often replies with Be3, f3 and Qd2, and plans to castle long.

moves.comment: The Dragon. Next the bishop goes to g7.

hints: Use a pawn.
It is the pawn on the g-file. Push it one square to g6.
steps.intro: White has played 5.Nc3. Black to move. Prepare the dragon bishop by pushing the g-pawn one square.

moves.comment: Castled. The king is safe and the rook comes to f8.

hints: Use your king.
Castle on the kingside: the king goes to g8.
steps.intro: White has played 7.f3. Black to move. Make your king safe by castling.

hints: The first move is a pawn on the c-file.
After the knight takes on d4, play Nf6, then the Dragon pawn to g6.
Bishop to g7, castle, then attack the knight on d4 with a knight.
steps.intro: Play the Dragon line as Black.

points: A first look only: the Dragon is sharp and White often attacks the king
Lichess calls it the Dragon Variation; the pawn shape on d6, e7, f7, g6, h7 is said to look like a dragon
The idea: after ...g6 the bishop goes to g7 and looks down the long diagonal
A common White plan is the Yugoslav Attack: Be3, f3, Qd2 and long castling, then pushing the h-pawn
Black counters with piece play on the c-file
Do not promise students that the Dragon is easy: it needs care
mistakes: Forgetting to castle quickly
Opening the h-file for White's rook without a plan
Playing the Dragon without knowing that White can attack the king
Moving the same piece twice in the opening
questions: Where does the bishop go after ...g6?
Which long diagonal does it use?
Why is it important for Black to castle early in this line?

moves.comment: The Old Sicilian. The knight is developed and watches d4.
Black takes the pawn.
White recaptures. Black will attack this knight again with pieces.

steps.intro: After 2.Nf3 Black has choices. The move 2...Nc6 puts a knight out and watches d4. The move 2...e6 opens the road for the f8 bishop. Here we show 2...Nc6.

moves.comment: The knight comes out and watches d4.

hints: Use a knight.
Move the knight on b8 to c6.
steps.intro: White has played 2.Nf3. Black to move. Develop the queenside knight to c6.

moves.comment: The pawn opens the diagonal for the f8 bishop.

hints: Use a pawn.
It is the pawn in front of the king. Push it one square to e6.
steps.intro: Same position. This time Black wants a solid setup that frees the f8 bishop. Push the e-pawn one square.

points: After 2.Nf3 Black does not have to play 2...d6
2...Nc6 develops a piece at once and eyes the d4 square; Lichess calls it the Old Sicilian
2...e6 is solid: it opens the f8 bishop and keeps a flexible pawn setup
Both moves are good choices when you want to learn plans instead of long lines
Show that the same ideas come back: take on d4, develop, castle, then use the c-file
mistakes: Moving the knight to c6 and then moving it again for no reason
Playing ...e6 and then forgetting to develop the bishop on f8
Mixing move orders without knowing what White can do
questions: Which square does a knight on c6 watch?
Which bishop does ...e6 free?
Which of the two moves puts a piece out first?

moves.comment: The Alapin.
Black strikes at the center and attacks e4.
The queen takes back.
Black develops a knight.
A normal move. Black goes on to develop, for example with Bg4.

steps.intro: With 2.c3 White prepares to play d4 with a pawn behind it. Black answers at once with 2...d5, hitting the e4 pawn.

moves.comment: Black hits the center at once.

hints: Use a pawn.
It is the d-pawn. Push it two squares to d5.
steps.intro: White has played 2.c3. Black to move. Attack the pawn on e4 with your d-pawn: push it two squares.

hints: Answer 1.e4 with a c-pawn move, then hit the center with a d-pawn move.
Take back on d5 with the queen.
After d4, develop the g8 knight.
steps.intro: Play the Alapin line as Black.

points: White avoids the Open Sicilian with 2.c3 and wants to play d4 with a pawn on c3 as support
Lichess calls it the Alapin Variation
Two good replies are 2...d5 and 2...Nf6
After 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 the queen is out early but is safe if Black develops with care
Stay calm: Black strikes at the center at once
Only the idea is taught here, not a long line
mistakes: Playing 2...d6, which gives White an easy d4; this course recommends 2...d5 or 2...Nf6
Moving the queen again and again after ...Qxd5
Forgetting to answer d4 with a developing move
questions: Which pawn does 2...d5 attack?
What does c3 prepare for White?
Why do we not want to let White have both pawns on c3 and d4 for free?

moves.comment: The Closed Sicilian.
Black develops a knight.
White prepares to fianchetto the bishop.
Black does the same.
Both bishops sit on long diagonals.
A quiet, balanced position. Both sides will develop the rest of their pieces and castle.

steps.intro: After 2.Nc3 White does not rush to open the center. Black can build a solid setup: knight to c6, pawn to g6, bishop to g7 and a pawn to d6.

moves.comment: A natural developing move.

hints: Use a knight.
Move the knight on b8 to c6.
steps.intro: White has played 2.Nc3. Black to move. Develop the queenside knight to c6.

hints: Answer 1.e4 with a c-pawn move, then bring out the b8 knight.
Prepare a fianchetto with a g-pawn move and the f8 bishop.
Finish with a pawn move one square on the d-file.
steps.intro: Play the Closed Sicilian setup as Black.

points: White develops the knight and usually avoids an early d4
Lichess calls it the Closed Sicilian
A common set-up for White is g3, Bg2 and d3, a quiet plan
Black can answer with a solid set-up of Nc6, g6, Bg7 and d6
It starts quietly, but White often attacks on the kingside later; the pieces matter more than the memory
Name the idea: both sides develop and castle before the middlegame fights
mistakes: Rushing to open the center when you are not ready
Forgetting to castle because the position looks quiet
Copying White's moves without checking threats
questions: Why is this game called closed?
Which squares does White's bishop on g2 watch?
Which black pieces are developed in the setup?

moves.comment: The break comes at once. The pawn attacks e4.
White takes.
Black takes back and the center is open for development.

steps.intro: A pawn break is a push that challenges the other side's pawns. In the Sicilian, ...d5 is a key break. It fights for the center and gives the pieces room. Usually Black first develops the pieces. Against 2.c3 the early ...d5 is the exception: White's c3 pawn takes the c3 square from the knight, so the knight cannot hit the queen.

moves.comment: The pawn is regained.

hints: Use your queen.
Take the pawn on d5 with the queen from d8.
steps.intro: White has taken on d5. Black to move. Win the pawn back by capturing on d5 with the queen.
A break works best when your pieces are ready to help. If the king is still in the center, the open lines can be dangerous.

points: A pawn break means pushing a pawn to challenge the enemy pawns
In many Sicilian set-ups Black waits until the pieces are ready, then plays ...d5 to free the game
Against the Alapin 2.c3, Black can do it at once with 2...d5 because White's pawn on c3 means a knight cannot go to c3 and hit the queen after ...Qxd5
Do not push ...d5 only because you can: check that the pieces are developed and the king is safe
Which pieces defend d5 changes in each line, so the coach should show it on the board
mistakes: Pushing d5 before the pieces are developed
Forgetting that the pawn must be protected after it moves
Pushing d5 when the king is still in the center
questions: Why does Black like to break with d5?
What should be ready before the break?
How can White respond to the pawn on d5?

moves.comment: White puts the king on c1.
The rook joins the half-open c-file, the file where White's king now lives. It is ready for when that file opens up.

steps.intro: Black traded the c-pawn early, so the c-file is half-open. The rook joins the half-open c-file, the file where White's king now lives. It is ready for when that file opens up. Look at the line.

moves.comment: The rook joins the half-open c-file.

hints: Use a rook.
Use the rook on a8 and move it to c8.
steps.intro: White has castled long. Black to move. Put the a8 rook on the half-open c-file.
The pawn on c5 took on d4 and was traded off. With no black pawn on the c-file, a black rook has a half-open file to use.

points: After ...cxd4 Black has no c-pawn, so the c-file is half-open for a black rook
In the Dragon with long castling by White, the king lives on the c-file side, so this file may matter later
Black's rook, bishop on g7 and knights work together against the white king
The line shown reaches Black's rook move ...Rc8
Lichess knows the line to 10...Rc8 as the Old Line of the Yugoslav Attack
Do not claim this line wins: it is a plan, not a trick
mistakes: Leaving the rooks on the back rank and never using the half-open file
Forgetting to trade White's attacking knight on d4
Starting a pawn storm without any support
questions: Why is the c-file half-open for Black?
Where does White's king stand after long castling?
Which black piece moves to the c-file?

moves.comment: Black develops with a threat against the knight on d4.

steps.intro: Here is a healthy Black setup. The knight and bishop are out, and the king is castled. Now the b8 knight attacks the white knight on d4.

moves.comment: The knight is developed and attacks the knight on d4.

hints: Use a knight.
Move the knight on b8 to c6.
steps.intro: White has played 8.Qd2. Black to move. Develop the b8 knight so that it attacks the white knight on d4.
Developed pieces and a safe king come first. Plans work best when all your pieces can help.

points: Keep this lesson practical
In the Dragon line shown, Black attacks White's d4 knight with ...Nc6 after castling
Make students list what is developed: Nf6, Bg7, and the king is castled
Warn that the Sicilian is sharp: both kings can be in danger and one tempo can matter
Qb6 ideas and pawn grabs are left out here because they need exact theory the coach should choose
mistakes: Moving the same piece twice while the king is still in the center
Grabbing pawns with the queen and falling behind in development
Playing a line from memory without asking what White threatens
Copying a plan from one setup into a different one
questions: Which black pieces are already developed here?
What does ...Nc6 attack?
What is the first question to ask when the opponent leaves the book?

moves.comment: A simple start: take the center pawn and develop.

steps.intro: Choose the Sicilian when you want an unbalanced game and are willing to learn plans. Start simple: answer 1.e4 with ...c5, develop your pieces and castle.
A small setup you understand is better than long lines you only half remember.

points: The Sicilian suits players who want a fight and are ready to learn plans
It is not a good choice if you do not want to study at all
You can start with a small setup, such as 2...Nc6 or 2...e6, and learn more later
Compare with 1...e5: that move is also good, just a different type of game
The coach decides the right time for each student
mistakes: Picking the Sicilian only because strong players do
Memorizing long lines and forgetting the plans
Being afraid of White's attacks and not castling
questions: Why might you choose the Sicilian?
What do you need to learn first?
Which second move gives you a simple start?
